title: Section 8 companies and tax-exempt status
summary: The Section 8 company, and what a not-for-profit must meet for public benefit status and tax exemption.

chunks.heading: The Section 8 company
chunks.explanation_md:
The Indian Companies Act allows certain companies to get not-for-profit status as **section 8 companies**.

- **Purpose**: formed for "promoting commerce, art, science, religion, charity or any other useful object", provided no profits or other income from promoting its objects are **distributed in any form to its members**.
- **Minimum**: **three individuals** to form it.
- **Application**: founders or promoters apply to the **Regional Director of the Company Law Board**, with copies of the proposed memorandum and articles of association, a **statement of assets** and a brief description of the work planned.
- **Governance**: similar to a society. It generally has members and is governed by directors, a managing committee or a governing council elected by the members.
- **Dissolution**: like a society (unlike a trust) it may be dissolved. After debts are settled, funds and property **may not be distributed among members**; they go to another Section 8 company, preferably with similar objects.

key_terms.meaning: A company with not-for-profit status; no profits or income may be distributed to members; at least three individuals form it.

chunks.heading: Public benefit status and tax exemption
chunks.explanation_md:
To be tax-exempt under the **Income Tax Act, 1961** (as amended by Finance Act, 2024), a not-for-profit entity must be organized for **religious or charitable purposes**. Charitable purposes include relief of the poor, education, medical relief and advancement of any other object of general public utility. Public charitable trusts must be created for public benefit, societies may be registered for charitable purposes, and Section 8 companies are formed for the limited purposes in their definition.

The slide gives the conditions:

- organized for religious or charitable purposes
- must **spend 85% of its income** in a financial year (April 1st to March 31st) on its objects, with **12 months** after year end to comply
- surplus income may be accumulated for specific projects for **1 to 5 years**
- no part of income or property may directly or indirectly benefit the founder, trustee, their relatives, or a person who contributed more than **Rs. 50,000** in a financial year
- the annual income return must be filed on time

questions.stem: Explain the Section 8 company and the conditions a not-for-profit must satisfy to enjoy tax exemption.
questions.model_answer_md:
A **Section 8 company** is a not-for-profit company under the Indian Companies Act, formed for promoting commerce, art, science, religion, charity or another useful object.

**Formation.** No profits or income from pursuing its objects may be distributed in any form to members. At least **three individuals** form it. The promoters apply to the **Regional Director of the Company Law Board** with copies of the memorandum and articles of association, a statement of assets and a short description of the proposed work.

**Governance and dissolution.** Governance is like a society: members elect directors, a managing committee or a governing council. It may be dissolved, and its remaining funds go to another Section 8 company, preferably with similar objects, not to members.

**Tax-exempt status.** Under the Income Tax Act, 1961, an entity must be organized for religious or charitable purposes, which include relief of the poor, education, medical relief and other objects of general public utility. It must spend **85% of its income** in the financial year (April 1st to March 31st) on its objects, with 12 months after year end to comply. Surplus can be accumulated for specific projects for 1 to 5 years. No part of income or property may benefit the founder, a trustee, their relatives or anyone who contributed more than Rs. 50,000 in the year. The annual income return must be filed on time.

In conclusion, a Section 8 company and other not-for-profit bodies keep their tax benefit only while profits serve the public purpose.
